items.body: Truth must be said from the beginning, I’m not, even a little, objective when it comes to John Coltrane’s last chapter in life and in music. Those two are inseparable in any case. Second truth is that this last period that starts roughly sometime in 1964, prior to A Love Supreme, and ends with his death is my favorite music. He and all his comrades, especially Alice, Pharoah, Rashied and Jimmy managed to create a body of music of transcendence –an ascension for the soul and deep meditation for the mind. My album of choice is this last live recording (where the aforementioned musicians are joined by Juma Santos and Algie DeWitt on percussion), recorded just three months before his death at the Olatunji Center of African Culture in Harlem, N.Y.C. In a quite symbolic move (the place: deep in an African-American neighborhood, the name: African Culture and tradition as a starting point) the music of the players, even though both geographically and in name still black, still jazz but free, is already a new entity. With this recording, one that the sound is not so hi-fi, Coltrane’s sound seems to be in the final stage of the total freedom that Ascension initiated. Listening to the unrelenting growls, howls and their thick wall of sound created by Trane and Pharoah, one could easily comment that the two tracks, Ogunde of almost half an hour and the total reconstruction of My Favorite Things that clocks in thirty four uncontrollably joyous minutes, are pure noise. This ferocious a la Ayler attack by the two locked in reeds brothers, provides a rough field, like a magic carpet flying in the air, for the others to give everything they have. And they have to give a lot to the not so big crowd attending, as their collective struggle to follow or lead at some points, or intertwine with small gestures like the polyrhythmic-not-so-rhythmic barrages by Rashied, the lovingly plucked piano chords by Alice and the even though not always audible, monstrous strength by Jimmy on double bass. Allow me to humbly comment that Coltrane’s music channeled everything in black tradition and went beyond that. He created his own tradition. You also don’t need me to say that this is an amazing recording. One that encapsulates all the stated goals by John Coltrane himself. Total freedom, love, myriads of feelings and a spiritual unity that could be the final Truth. If there’s something to think about, to question, it could be this: where could his music go after this? Did he, before even turning 41, reached a point of no return? @fot.isn Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是约翰·科川去世前三个月在哈莱姆奥拉通吉非洲文化中心录制的现场录音，与妻子Alice、次中音萨克斯手Pharoah、鼓手Rashied及贝斯手Jimmy等乐手共同完成。录音虽非高保真，但完整呈现了科川晚期追求的解放状态音乐理念。《Ogunde》以接近半小时的时长让双萨克斯形成互锁的咆哮与嘶吼声墙，而《My Favorite Things》的彻底重构则以三十四分钟的自由即兴展开。在这片充满力量与张力的粗糙音景之上，Alice的钢琴和弦拨奏、Rashied的多节奏打击纹理以及Jimmy的低音贝斯为整体提供了支撑框架。作品体现了科川对黑人音乐传统的吸收与超越，将非洲文化根基与完全即兴的集体对话融为一体，展现出精神性的统一力量。

items.body: Over the past five years, Philip Samartzis has been building a body of distinct work. The interrelated recordings are identifiable by their adjacent titles: 2021’s Polar Force / Array (with Eugene Ughetti); 2023’s Atmospheres and Disturbances; 2024’s Air Pressure (with Michael Vorfeld); and now 2026’s Atmospheric Pressure, again with Vorfeld. The starting point for these ventures was a pair of residencies sponsored by the Australian Antarctic Territory Arts Fellowship program. Samartzis was able to capture some incredible recordings in sub-zero temperatures, and they have proven to be a wealth of material in both pure and sculpted forms. As on Air Pressure, Samartzis contributes electronics, Vorfeld stringed instruments and percussion. The new set zeroes in on a 36-hour blizzard at the Casey Research Station in 2016. Amid the hundred-knot winds and white-out conditions, “the station was reduced to pressure, vibration, and sound.” Simply picturing David Nielson’s cover image of David Ward inspecting dog lines in 1990, one can already feel the cold and intuit the level of difficulty. “Gravitational Overflow” sets the stage with slowly increasing winds and the creak of vanes (personified by Vorfeld’s instruments). The wind and snow create their own music, an undulating drone of literal white noise. Percussion enters as sympathetic partner; one imagines the rattling of glass and iron, caught in a maelstrom of Biblical proportions. Toward the end, these metallic pats and taps take center stage, as if representing the eye of the hurricane. “Depression” refers to atmospheric conditions, although one would be forgiven for thinking that it might mirror a mood. The isolation of research stations often produces feelings of malaise. The electronics and radio chatter are surprises in the wake of the opener; some portions even sound like turntable scratches or graffiti cans being shaken. The focus is not on the machine hum and motor sputter, but instead, what happens when the electricity fails. The purely percussive section arrives earlier, in the sixth minute, like the last sounds of a man caught in a storm, having lost all bearings, facing death by making music one last time, his only audience the abyss. “Cold Front” reveals the full depth of the danger. The strings seem as agitated as the snow, the percussion as frozen as the sleet, the electronics as charged as the air. Sound bends around the cymbals like sheets of ice. In the sixth minute, a sound like clomping hooves comes across like a phantasm. The actual storm mixes with the impression of the storm to convey feelings of being trapped inside or wandering outside: stir crazy or snow-blind. The applause at the very end is well-earned. We’re not sure how many more Antarctic recordings Samartzis has in the bag, but as so few of us are likely to hear them in person, each release arrives as a revelation. (Richard Allen)
items._genre: experimental / field recording / drone / ambient / electroacoustic
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是Samartzis与Vorfeld合作的延续，素材源自2016年Casey研究站36小时暴风骤停的现场录音。Samartzis贡献电子声学处理，Vorfeld提供弦乐与打击乐。专辑以现场录音与电子处理为基础，通过缓慢增强的风声、旗帜振动与金属敲击构建持续音景。打击乐以共鸣方式介入，与白噪音形成对话；电子元素与无线电杂音制造停电后的荒凉感；弦乐被处理得如同冰层般冷冽。整体呈现出被困室内与户外迷失的双重感知，将极地科考站的孤立感转化为声音体验。乐评认为这种将自然录音与乐器演奏融合的手法具有独特的揭示意义，延续了Samartzis自南极艺术奖学金以来的创作脉络。

items.body: Review by Logan — Going back to Hi Scores after spending much time with the heavy, dark sound of Inferno acts like finding an old, clean blueprint before it got weathered. This 1996 EP finds the Sandison brothers at a time when their geometric tracking methods were still sharp and exposed, before getting heavily into deep analogue erosion. It occupies a unique place in their discography, throwing out the fragile sentimentality of their later records. It sounds like a raw, intense sonicenvironment rather than a piece of electronic escapism. It follows an internal logic that matches how my own mind wants to navigate structure, maintaining an unbroken hold throughout the short-form layout.The record starts off with the clinical drive of the title track, "Hi Scores". Spending time with their wider catalogue highlights how unique this upfront electro-funk grid is. Originally released on Manchester's experimental Skam label, it sets up a stark, unpolished baseline belonging to the sharp mathematical grids of the mid-nineties IDM scene rather than a cozy childhood memory. It reveals a naked skeletal frame, showing their basic programming choices before they began burying their arrangements in rich, atmospheric grime.The sequence drops immediately into "Turquoise Hexagon Sun", which remains a deeply resonant track. Knowing how this piece functions later on Music Has the Right to Children makes its placement here feel even more striking. It introduces the loop-based geometry and hexagonal motifs they would keep referencing for decades. Yet, for all its melodic layers, it holds a weird, slightly unsettling friction. It is a track I routinely turn off when the kids are around, since the underlying textures feel less like a comforting memory and more like a displaced, menacing transmission.Because I know the organic transitions of Music Has the Right to Children inside and out, what happens next forces a mental gear-shift. Instead of a soft fade, the drop into "Nlogax" is a sharp, jarring choice that feels almost surgically implanted into the record. The track triggers a heavy physical response in my system; the microtonal dissonance and aggressive, detuned synth hook warp the stereo field until it gives a genuine sensation of vertigo and physical nausea.Without giving a chance to recover, "June 9th" steps straight out of that pitch instability and into a state of sensory hyper-vigilance. By layering skittering, fast percussion elements over a lagging breakbeat and burying muffled melodies under a massive low-end thrum, the duo compresses the perception of space, locking my senses inside a claustrophobic acoustic panic room. While playing this track, I found myself comparing its complex, cinematic logic to The Future Sound of London's 1994 masterpiece, Lifeforms. Both share that same uncompromising, alien architectural layout that rejects simple dancefloor trends. On a surface listen, Hi Scores can seem far more disjointed than it actually is, but sitting immersed in this middle section shows how every single segment serves a rigid purpose. There is no randomness here.The sheer intensity of these tracks left me blown away. I was deeply wowed by the experience, and it is fascinating to realise that this personal state of shock links directly to the literal mechanical wow and flutter effect running through the tape machines. The severe pitch warps build an environment that is intensely suffocating, forcing a raw, physical confrontation across my enteric nervous system.The record begins to rewire my neural pathways during "Seeya Later". Having tracked its connection back to Twoism, I notice how it works on an interesting psychological plane here, utilising heavy, drifting synth pads to tie the upfront grooves to the end of the record, pulling my brain down into a heavy twilight trance.The closing slot belongs to "Everything You Do Is a Balloon", which serves as a definitive thesis statement for their subsequent discography. In this non-sentimental context, however, the track offers little safe haven or comforting relief. It feels off-kilter and stripped of safety, trading easy nostalgia for an overwhelming, earth-shaking sonic power. Starting with that fragile, beautifully melancholic synth melody before dropping into a heavy, slow-motion hip-hop breakbeat, it functions not as a comforting exit, but as a towering, visceral climax that carries the electro-acoustic DNA that would decades later anchor the dense harmonic textures of The Campfire Headphase.Ultimately, Hi Scores stands as an uncomfortable five-star masterpiece, acting more like a raw template for psychological disruption than a standard piece of auditory expression. Spending time with all of their albums only reinforces how essential this blueprint is. I so appreciate and deeply experience absolutely everything on this record, and it sits as something perfect for my specific internal architecture. In fact, this is a six out of five star release for me. It is intense, it is disorienting, and it is utterly brilliant.

items._cn_summary: 这是一张1996年发行的EP，记录了Boards of Canada兄弟早期尚未被浓厚模拟质感包裹的状态。标题曲以临床感的电声放克网格切入，呈现出九十年代中叶IDM场景特有的锋利数学结构，而非后期作品那种怀旧氛围。第二曲沿用了后来在经典专辑中发展的循环几何与六角形动机，但此处保留着一种不安的摩擦感与被错置的传输质地。第三、四首则陡然切入微音程不和谐与失谐合成器钩子，制造出听觉上的眩晕与生理上的压迫感，快速打击元素与延迟碎拍叠加闷响旋律，在低频轰鸣中压缩空间感，形成幽闭的声学体验。整张作品遵循一套内在逻辑，呈现出裸露的骨架般的基础编程选择，与该组合后期丰满的编曲美学形成鲜明对照。

items.body: Review by Fercandio46 — It is no coincidence that many electronic music artists draw inspiration from the past, specifically the 1970s. The British duo Boards of Canada creates a sound that feels progressive in an electronic sense, much like the Norwegian duo R�yksopp has done at times. It is the art of layering sounds, not haphazardly, but with a very clear purpose: to evoke moods and suggest mental images or ideas that often transcend mere musical concepts. The cover of their debut album, Music Has the Right to Children, always struck me as very retro, very 1960s, yet upon closer inspection, much like a painting bearing an artist's signature, one discovers that the figures lack actual faces. They are blank slates, leaving the viewer to imagine what lies within. "An Eagle in Your Mind" offers a magnetic groove, featuring a downtempo rhythm with a strong, minimalist trip-hop foundation. The track combines an organic drum feel with the presence of both samples and scratching, making it highly appealing and modern; it also reminds me of another underground classic, Vernon Reid's first solo album, Mistaken Identity (1996), which blended heavy guitar work with electronic elements and featured DJ Logic.Short tracks like "The Color of the Fire" reminded me, in the spaces between the longer pieces, of the intros on Gong's Angel's Egg, as well as the poetic ambient atmospheres of Brian Eno. The use of analog synthesizers also draws a parallel to another electronic duo, the French group Air, and in "Telephasic Workshop," we can observe how two parallel paths, traced by Michael Sandison and Marcus Eoin respectively, overlap: one line is a steady, unwavering, and steadfast drone, while the other plays solos and varies, confident in the support of its stable counterpart."Sixtyten" is spacey and psychedelic, yet syncopated; the ghostly voices lending mystery to the final mix appear like palace spies straight out of Hieronymus Bosch's The Garden of Earthly Delights. I find funk and jazz elements in Turquoise Hexagon Sun; ambient music can be that rich, Brian Eno knows a lot about that, too, and his spirit is present on this album as well. It's about not being afraid to experiment and treating music like water: if it spills, it doesn't disappear, it simply changes shape.The bridges turn into short songs in their own right, tracks with their own distinct identity, such as "Kaini Industries" or "Bocuma", a synthesizer part that can evoke a natural waterfall, or statues coming to life at night... and "Roygbiv," which fuses a hip-hop beat with a highly symphonic, atmospheric mood, yet possesses just the right touch to feel fresh, almost New Wave, thanks to a simple keyboard, like those three-prong outlets. "Rue The Whirl" represents the brand of progressive electronica that appeals to me most; its tension builds steadily, an electronic record charged with alternating current. Through waves of sound, it achieves a passive, psychedelic atmosphere, almost a trance state, yet one not devoid of variation, as it ultimately flirts with dissonance and details like Mellotrons, striking the perfect balance between the vintage and the postmodern.The secret behind the change in sound, so percussive and featuring a sort of equidistant echo, in "Aquarius" is a slap-funk sample from the song of the same name from the movie Hair (1979). The narrative voice, the children's laughter, reminiscent of what Rickie Lee Jones used on her album Pop Pop, and those percussive variations combined to create a hybrid that was also hypnotic. Pete Standing Alone returns to those minimalist Brian Eno-esque melodies, but incorporates samples that introduce variations and shifts in rhythm, preventing the listener from settling into a routine, as the aim is to keep the sonic progression moving forward."Smokes Quantity" is rhythm with substance, a melody that provokes and leaves a lasting mark, keeping the mind wide awake; Boards of Canada offers an inward journey that challenges one's comfort zone, much like atonal music once did. Only then are we ready for "Open the Light," with its emotive, Vangelis-esque progression, for it is wrong to skip chapters that were sequenced in a specific order to prime the mood and ensure receptiveness to the climax of the penultimate track, experiencing it for what it truly is: a sonic journey.
items._genre: downtempo electronic / ambient / IDM / trip-hop
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑以层层叠叠的采样和模拟合成器构建出怀旧而超现实的声景，介于氛围音乐与智识舞曲之间。乐评指出其声音设计并非随意堆砌，而是以唤起情绪和暗示意象为目的。慢速节拍配合有机鼓感与唱机刮擦，形成磁性的律动基础。短小曲目作为长曲间的呼吸空间，带有诗歌般的氛围特质。不同曲目展现出多样的融合倾向：迷幻太空感的声效与幽灵般的人声采样、爵士放克元素的隐性渗入、嘻哈节拍与交响化氛围的交织，以及通过持续嗡鸣与变化独奏形成对话式的双线结构。模拟合成器的运用赋予整体温暖而复古的质感，与法国电子双人组Air的声响美学形成呼应。整张专辑以渐进式的张力构建和波形声浪，营造出被动的迷幻氛围。

items.body: Reading back into the reviews of this recording, from over the past decades, you encounter the word “relentless” a lot, probably more than for any other album in the history of albums. It’s interesting because, when I first heard Interstellar Space , “relentless” was the word that occurred to me — right after the introductory bells of track one faded. Till then, I hadn’t realized that “relentless” was a thing that music could be, and that relentlessness was awesome. Even transcendent. It’s not a complicated record. You’ve got your tenor and drums. Each piece starts with a theme, enters the improvisation, and then winds down and restates the theme. Each improvisation travels a similar arc, beginning in a saner space, rising intensity and ecstasy, whipping us into a frenzy, then easing off into … well, not serenity, but you get close to it as you hear the shaken bells that begin the next piece. The joys of Interstellar Space come not from structural intrigue, but from the cascadingly brilliant improvs. Coltrane and Ali were both ridiculously ON that day. (Ali actually felt he had underperformed because he didn’t know they were doing a duet session until he arrived at the session.) And the duet setting makes the music almost transparent. Aside from the beauty of Trane and Ali’s playing, you also get a sense of exactly what Coltrane was trying for. His insistent explorations (relentless) are laid bare. This is an excellent entry to Coltrane’s later works. His playing is like water moving through the ground, trying to find its way through a shelf of granite. Eventually, the water finds the crevices, freezes, expands, thaws, and breaks the stone to pieces. The water always wins. A force of nature. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook
items._genre: free jazz / avant-garde / spiritual jazz / improvisation
items._cn_summary: 这张1974年的专辑是Coltrane晚期作品的精华，以萨克斯与鼓的二重奏形式呈现，每首曲目遵循主题—即兴—回归主题的结构。乐评指出，即兴段落的弧线从理性出发，逐步攀升至强度与狂喜的顶峰，随后在铃声引入下一首时缓缓回落。Coltrane与鼓手Rashied Ali在录音当天状态极佳，二重奏的极简编制让音乐几乎透明，Coltrane后期作品中那种执拗的探索本质得以毫无遮蔽地呈现。Ali直到录音当天才得知是二重奏录制，这种意外的偶然性反而促成了高度敏锐的现场回应。乐评将其音乐比作穿透花岗岩的水流——持续的、不可阻挡的自然之力。这张专辑适合作为进入Coltrane晚期作品的入口。

items.album: Rachel Shearer ~ Te Oro a te Ao
items.excerpt: Black album covers are fairly rare; Prince’s The Black Album comes to mind, along with Thembi Soddell’s black-on-black Love Songs, which includes a book of black print on black pages. items.body: Black album covers are fairly rare; Prince’s The Black Album comes to mind, along with Thembi Soddell’s black-on-black Love Songs, which includes a book of black print on black pages. Rachel Shearer is the latest addition to this small group, as Te Oro a te Ao (the resounding of the world) presents black type on a black background. The hue honors Hinenuitepō, the goddess of night and death, and issues a warning on climate change. Shearer reflects her Aotearoan (New Zealand) roots by translating the Māori concept of whakapapa into aural form. The belief that all of nature, including time, is connected forms the basis of this work. The opening “Waha” (featuring Cathy Livermore) means both gate and voice, and serves as an entry point not only to the album, but to the spiritual world. It arrives as an invocation or incantation, at first a cappella, then layered, then sanded with dirt, dust and rock. Over time it becomes a choir, its sedimentary layers accumulating until they solidify into a drone. Is this the earth speaking, or our ancestors, or the buzz of time? The collective sound overtakes the individual without sublimating her power. The heart of the album is the two-part “Pounamu Becoming Crystal.” The first part reflects the “movement and strength of water,” which begins as a mist yet transforms into a torrent. While experiencing such dynamic contrast, one may think of everything from the act of creation to the destruction of the planet. The piece incorporates “subterranean volcanic activity, tectonic plate movements and land slippages,” and acts as a parable of disruption. Yet by the end, the timbres soften, offering a modicum of hope; perhaps time’s arrow is instead a cycle. The second segment, subtitled “Wiriwiri” (to tremble), honors the dance of Tānerore: the visible shimmer of hot air as it rises from the ground. At first, the piece continues the rumbling timbres of its predecessor, but these give way to white noise: the processed sound of cicadas, whose volume increases with the temperature. As Earth warms, the cries of the cicadas grow ever more insistent. “Ao” is a flexible word that can mean “sunrise,” “clouds” or even “world.” This gentle guitar coda suggests a manner of living on the planet, honoring sound with sound, presence with presence, gift with gift. While this is the Māori way, it is not often replicated, especially in Western societies. The arc of the album – invitation, experience, farewell – suggests a mode of interaction that posits all creation, animate and inanimate, as partners, the breath of heat mingling with the breath of life, the audible with the inaudible, the present with the absent and the yet-to-come. (Richard Allen)
items._genre: experimental / ambient / drone / world fusion / field recording
items._cn_summary: Rachel Shearer 的《Te Oro a te Ao》将毛利文化中的 whakapapa（万物互联）观念转化为听觉形式。专辑以黑色设计致敬夜晚女神 Hinenuitepō，同时暗含对气候变化的警示。开场曲《Waha》以清唱为起点，层层叠加人声并混入泥土、尘埃与岩石的质感，最终汇聚为持续的嗡鸣声响，模糊了个人与集体、人类与大地之间的界限。核心曲目《Pounamu Becoming Crystal》两部分分别以水的涌动与蝉鸣白噪音为载体，呈现从蒸汽到洪流、从低频轰鸣到渐强嘶鸣的动态变化。终曲《Ao》以简洁的吉他收束，呼应日出、世界与云的多重含义。整张专辑遵循邀请、体验、告别的弧线结构，试图重建一种将所有造物视为伙伴的感知方式。

items.body: Review by Logan — The Past Inside the FutureI feel Boards of Canada may speak more to people who are wired for math and geometric sequences. If an audience approaches their music looking for standard progressive showmanship or rapid chord changes, it could sound like background noise or simple down-tempo loops. But sitting with it can reveal a thoughtful, structural design. Even back on this 1995 release, they were already embedding things like the Fibonacci sequence and the golden ratio into the tracking layout, treating their loops less like pop filler and more like circular equations.Twoism works especially well for me because of its bookends. The opening track, "Sixtyniner", introduces a quiet vocal sample about seeing the future and the past. It's clear this isn't just an isolated early experiment; it's the literal seed for how the brothers deliberately engineer their past directly into their future compositions -- a blueprint they would call back to years later when looping the phrase "the past inside the present" on Geogaddi's "Music Is Math".This way of looping time parallels David Lynch and Angelo Badalamenti's Twin Peaks. The tracks across Twoism move a lot like the Lodge -- a space built on drifting tape loops, hidden rhythms, and warped vocal cues that blur the line between backward and forward movement. Instead of using flashy soloing for surprise, the music relies on a disciplined, eerie repetition to hold a twilight mood. That heavy atmosphere resolves in the closer, ""Smokes Quantity / 1986 Summer Fire", which drags a slow hip-hop beat through a dusty, tape-decayed claustrophobia that feels lost in time.Following the opener, "Oirectine" stands out as one of the most rewarding rhythmic tracks here. It drives a syncopated down-tempo pulse that shows, I think, that this era was not just some sleepy ambient wallpaper.The title track, "Twoism", is another favourite piece from the middle section. It sits right in the middle of the record with a murky, drifting sound built on unpolished, pitch-degraded synth pads. It doesn't break the established mood at all. It just adds a nice, heavy layer to the EP, showing that the core of the album has real musical weight instead of just filling space between the major tracks.The rest of the middle section plays out as a collection of shorter sketches and beat experiments grouped around the title track. Things like "Iced Cooly" and "Melissa Juice" work as quick, fragile moments built on slightly warped melodies that disappear before they can overstay their welcome. This lighter side balances against the rough drive of "Basefree", which drops a harsh, industrial beat that pushes closer to an unpolished techno sound. "Seeya Later" keeps that murky Lodge mood, using drifting synth pads to tie the upfront grooves to the end of the record. Instead of a standard checklist, these tracks work together as a collective landscape of early tracking ideas, holding things together before the closing architecture locks it all back into place.While at Rate Your Music I will give this a 3.5, for Prog Archives I give it a 3. I adore the opening and closing tracks ("Sixtyniner" and "Smokes Quantity / 1986 Summer Fire"), and very much like material in between, but I don't think it would as essential as many other releases for most. I would say if you are fan of Boards of Canada then this very likely is an essential piece of its history, and various of these tracks would be essential to my Boards of Canada compilation album. That ending does just make me want to listen to it all over again.
items._genre: downtempo / electronic / ambient / IDM
items._cn_summary: 这张1995年发行的EP展现了Boards of Canada早期对循环结构与数学序列的执着——将斐波那契数列与黄金比例嵌入曲目排列中，把loop视为环形方程而非流行填充。开篇曲以"看见未来与过去"的语音采样奠定整张作品的种子式概念，这一线索在多年后的Geogaddi中被显式调用。整体氛围与Twin Peaks中的Lodge空间呼应，依靠纪律化的重复与回声制造暮色感而非炫技段落。标题曲目以失谐的合成器pad构成浑浊的中段核心，"Basefree"则引入粗粝的工业节拍推向不修边幅的techno边缘，"Seeya Later"用飘移的pad将前后连接起来，"Smokes Quantity/1986 Summer Fire"以磁带衰变的封闭感作结。整体呈现为一片由早期跟踪构想组成的连续声景，适合耐心聆听的听众。

items.body: Arcana Magna Silentia Cold Meat Industry The fourteen year gap between Swedish neo-classical/dark ambient project Arcana’s As Bright As A Thousand Suns and new LP Magna Silentia was marked by halted reactivations, live reunions, and tremendous personal loss for Peter and Cecilia Bjärgö and their collaborators. It’s no surprise, then, to find them working in a register quite different from their last recorded material, though Magna Silentia‘s combination of Arcana’s earliest and most austere work and the technical prowess they’ve since accrued makes for a striking and affecting reemergence. Records like Thousand Suns and Raspail saw an expansion of Arcana’s acoustic side, augmenting their neo-classical side with folk threads which resulted in a sound not unlike mid-period Dead Can Dance. That degree of ornamentation has been stripped back Magna Silentia. Low, abyssal horns and drones accompany ritual drums whose earthy timbre carries real menace on “The Adversity Bell”, yet the melodic thread of the piece, carried almost exclusively by Peter’s wordless vocals, is far more frail and pained than those more bracing elements might suggest. And it’s in that tension, between the severity of a record which fittingly marks Arcana’s return to Cold Meat Industry (and everything that infamous label entails) and the full, crushing emotional register of real human grief and loss, that Magna Silentia shines. A sustained focus on funereal dark ambient drones and echoes is often the conduit for that tension. Dark ambient has always been one part of Arcana’s heady alchemy to be sure, but it’s never been given so much focus as it has here. The rich sound design and subtle but elegant compositional chops which guide “Somnia Intus” might not have been achievable for Bjärgö in the project’s early years, but are now well within his grasp and fit the record’s sober and enduring grief. While perhaps more abstract and less directly emotional, “The Obsidian Mirror” again finds Arcana wielding both metallic, industrial noise and contemplative tones in equilibrium (for a project which has always focused on atmosphere they’ve rarely felt “cinematic” in the way that term’s often deployed, yet there’s something of a classic cyberpunk cityscape in this track). For all of its pain and extremity, there are real currents of beauty in Magna Silentia. The mournful violin which passes through glowing chorales in “The Collapsing Of All Light” might not be as bombastic as some of Arcana’s earlier neo-classical works, but it’s as affecting as any of them. After their hiatus Arcana have returned to their roots, shaped by time and loss, but none the weaker for it. Recommended. Buy it. Magna Silentia by Arcana The post Arcana, “Magna Silentia” appeared first on I Die: You Die.
items._genre: dark ambient / neo-classical / industrial / ritual
items._cn_summary: 瑞典项目 Arcana 在沉寂十四年后推出的新作，融合了早期作品中简朴严峻的暗潮氛围与多年累积的成熟技艺。专辑以低沉的号角与持续嗡鸣的无人机为核心，配合带有泥土质感的仪式鼓点，形成压迫感与脆弱人声之间的张力。评论指出，这种张力源自创作者经历的真实丧失与悲痛，使音乐在抽象的黑暗环境声响中承载了厚重的情感重量。作品回归了早年合作的厂牌 Cold Meat Industry 的美学，同时展现了丰富的声音设计与细腻的编曲能力。哀伤的弦乐在合唱中穿行，与工业噪音和冥想式的音色交织，呈现出电影般的广阔声景。整张专辑虽充满痛楚与极端，但同时流淌着深沉的美感，是一次经历时间与失落淬炼后的回归。

items.body: It Was A Time Of Laboured Metaphors Australia-born, Belfast-based artist Kate Carr’s musical work can be divided into two rough categories: place-based explorations using field recordings made in a specific location, such as 2014’s “Overheard in Doi Saket”, featuring sounds captured in Thailand, or last year’s “I Had Myself A Nuclear Spring”, inspired by wetlands surrounding the imposing presence of a nuclear power station in France; and albums that seem to refer less to a specific place than to personal narratives, for instance the emotional depths of “Fabulations”. On closer examination, however, such a distinction turns out to be overly simplistic, as most simple binaries tend to be, with the ostensibly location-oriented work foregrounding a specifically personal response to a given site, and the more abstract work mapping out a series of points in an interior and exterior travelogue. In many ways, Carr’s new album “It Was A Time Of Laboured Metaphors” takes the more abstract, dreamlike qualities of “Fabulations” a step or two further. Gone completely now are the trademark guitar melodies that were an instantly-recognisable hallmark of her sound for many years. The haunting synth, rough noises, and clicking static that hovered in the background of “Fabulations” now form the essence of a stripped-back and bare music. Field recordings are still present, but their function seems entirely changed: no longer simple markers of place or carriers of narrative, the echoing voices, clunking goats’ bells, skateboarders, and even chirruping birds instead serve as a sort of counterbalance to the maudlin, sometimes downright gloomy atmospheres created by the low drones and echoing pops and cracks. When the music seems to be getting sucked too far down the hole of introspection, these found sounds intervene to place the pathos in the context of a world that encompasses and exceeds it. If, as she suggests in her artist’s statement, Carr’s music centres on the question of how we come to know ourselves through sound and place, then with its quietness, dark colours, and frequent hesitations, “It Was A Time” seems like an album made for the lonelier, emptier moments of translocation. Those “What am I doing here?” moments are familiar enough to anyone who has travelled. With this music, Carr shows a continued willingness to be open and listen, even to such moments. The sounds inhabit a world more concrete grey and mundane than bright and exotic, but this didn’t spoil my enjoyment of them — perhaps music made for the place in which you are is preferable to a mirage of implausible escape? In any case, “It Was A Time” makes for a deep and absorbing night-time listen.     Kate Carr The Helen Scarsdale Agency
items._genre: ambient / field recording / drone / experimental
items._cn_summary: Kate Carr的新专辑延续了她以田野录音为核心的声音探索，但相比以往更抽象、更内省。吉他元素被完全剥离，合成器、低频嗡鸣、粗糙噪音和静电声构成音乐的主体，田野录音的功能也发生转变——回声、山羊铃、滑板声、鸟鸣等不再是地标式的叙事载体，而是作为外部世界的参照，与音乐内部的忧郁氛围形成对话。评论指出，这种处理方式将内心的情绪波动放置于更广阔的现实语境中，使其不至于陷入纯粹的自省。这张作品呈现出安静、灰暗、犹疑的气质，适合独自旅行或身处陌生环境时的夜晚聆听，声音世界偏向平凡而非奇幻，但正是这种平凡感赋予了作品真实的存在感。

items.body: The broadly ambitious Generate Music is the Prism Quartet's latest project, featuring saxophonists Timothy McAllister (soprano), Zachary Shemon (alto), Matthew Levy (tenor), and Taimur Sullivan (baritone). Formed in 1984, their mission is �To place the saxophone in unexpected contexts, expand the repertoire through new commissions, and challenge audiences.� On this eleven-track, 86-minute set, they do just that. Tyshawn Sorey | Ursula Rucker | Diane Monroe This collection includes the quartet augmented by David Gilmore (Electric guitar), David Krakauer (Klezmer clarinet), Tyshawn Sorey (Drums and percussion), Reuben Rogers (Bass), Ursula Rucker (Vocals and poetry), Susan Watts (Trumpet and vocals), and Diane Monroe (Violin). Through modern jazz arrangements, improvisations,� and spoken word, they seek to �explore the historical, cultural, and creative ties between Black and Jewish Americans.� Generate Music by PRISM Quartet, D. Gilmore, D. Krakauer, D. Monroe, R. Rogers, U. Rucker, T. Sorey, S. Watts � The opening track references �A Griot and a Cantor,� the storyteller in West African culture and the worship leader in the Jewish faith. The sonic architecture arrives with �The Unknown Common Ancestor,� which jumps between a World Saxophone Quartet-inspired sound and klezmer music with clarinet and trumpet.� � Generate Music by PRISM Quartet, D. Gilmore, D. Krakauer, D. Monroe, R. Rogers, U. Rucker, T. Sorey, S. Watts The striking and authoritative voice of Ursula Rucker narrates �Requiem for AJ.� After a dramatic overture, it sets up the narrative tension that develops across the record. Rucker tells the story of the 1964 murders of civil rights activists James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner near Philadelphia, Mississippi. On the 60th anniversary of this American tragedy, Rucker explains that they went �to register black voters (sigh)� and then she asks us to: Look up the rest of the story if you care Do you... Care? Or do you just... Do you?� With tense dramatic irony, Rucker nonchalantly states, �Poets have queries,� and the recitation ends with emphatic repetition of �Do you?�� This ten-minute powerhouse also features the band at its best with Tyshawn Sorey�s swirling drumming and David Gilmore (not to be confused with his Pink Floyd namesake) offering one of his several fiery guitar solos. It makes a fitting single, representative of the in-your-face right-left punches of improvised jazz and honest stylized performance poetry. Generate Music by PRISM Quartet, D. Gilmore, D. Krakauer, D. Monroe, R. Rogers, U. Rucker, T. Sorey, S. Watts Highlighted throughout with bursts of klezmer, often seamlessly blended with funky jazz, the Jewish tradition is especially highlighted on �Lift Every Voice and Sing.� Originally debuted in 1900, this hymn by brothers John Rosamond Johnson and James Weldon Johnson has been called a �Negro national anthem.� Here it is translated into Yiddish by Joshua Woletzshky and sung by Susan Watts, featuring violin by Diane Monroe. �Shall I continue to lie about my sadness to keep you from yours?� asks Rucker on �Let�s All Gather & Go All Together, Shall We,� offering an optimistic way forward in a world of hate. She narrates the story of a young black man in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, who is murdered by a Jewish pharmacist, exposing grief but also a way to get beyond it. Here and throughout, the music comments, prods, replies, and exuberantly jams out. Powerful, virtuosic, and close to the bone, Generate Music keeps its promise and takes another giant step in the evolution of the Prism Quartet. "Let us gather and all go together" by Ursula Rucker Live at World Cafe, Philadelphia on June 8, 2024 Find the artist online. items._cn_summary: Prism Quartet 联合多位客座音乐人，推出这张探索非裔与犹太裔美国人历史、文化与创作纽带的概念专辑。作品以现代爵士编排、即兴演奏与诗歌朗诵交织，开篇在克莱兹默与世界萨克斯四重团式的声响之间跳跃。《Requiem for AJ》以十分钟篇幅回溯1964年民权运动悲剧，Ursula Rucker 的朗诵充满戏剧张力，Tyren Sorey 的鼓击与David Gilmore 的吉他独奏形成强烈对位。犹太传统元素与放克爵士无缝融合，克莱兹默段落不断闪现。整体制作打破常规四重奏配置，融合小提琴、单簧管、人声、诗歌与电子吉他，构建出兼具历史厚重与当代实验色彩的声音叙事。

items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.
items.label: Cool Waters
items._genre: folktronica / world fusion / experimental electronic / African traditional
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由内罗毕厂牌Cool Waters发行，是德国肯尼亚驻地打击乐手Sven Kacirek与Olith Ratengo、83岁传统肯尼亚歌手Ogoya Nengo的首次三方合作。Kacirek以Buchla合成器、手打打击乐和架子鼓构建音乐骨架，与两位人声形成对话。电子音色层叠渐进，复节奏悄悄潜入，最终与声线融为一体，既不掩盖传统根源，也赋予古老的dodo歌唱以当代质感。83岁歌手的全球首秀与电子节奏形成跨代碰撞，根脉成为先锋，革新看似亘古。专辑展现了文化间真诚对话而不践踏传统的可能性，是非洲与世界电子场景交汇的典型范例。

items.artist: Dorothy Moskowitz & United States of Alchemy
items.excerpt:
Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release,
Under an Endless Sky
.
In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari,
Songs of Compassion
is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics.
Francesco Paolo Paladi
items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. items.body: The Australian band Chiron is back with their latest album, a project three years in the making. Led by frontman Michael Aliani (ex-IKON) and joined by bassist Dino Molinaro (IKON) and guitarist Ivan Bullock, the band presents nine tracks plus four additional remixes. Those familiar with Chiron will hardly be surprised by the influences and style: the music is a fusion of Dark-Wave and Post-Punk. The dark atmosphere that permeates the album occasionally evokes memories of Joy Division, with a pervasive sense of darkness and melancholy running throughout. The guitar sometimes takes on a psychedelic edge, adding an interesting touch, while the synth elements provide an additional melodic dimension. Yvette Winkler (Vaselyne) was invited to collaborate on the final track. The additional remixes are far from ordinary; one of them, for instance, features vocals from the cold and charismatic Kriistal Ann (Paradox Obscur). They lean slightly more towards Electro, at times incorporating a more club-oriented vibe. Chiron has never disappointed me, and with “A Dark Beauty”, the band has once again delivered a top-notch album. Personally, however, I have a particular soft spot for the slightly heavier tracks. (Rating:8). Listen to “A Dark Beauty”: A Dark Beauty by Chiron About Chiron Chiron formed in Melbourne, Australia, in 1997, founded by vocalist Michael Aliani after he left the Australian darkwave band Ikon. The project debuted with “Eve” in 1999 on the Italian label Energeia, followed by “Slipping Away” (2005, Apollyon Records), the “Breaking Point” EP (2009) and the album “We Own the Night” (2015). A compilation, “Chiron: The Best Of”, appeared on Brazil’s Wave Records the same year. The band’s 2022 album “The Sun Goes Down” marked its move to Dark Vinyl Records and brought founding Ikon bassist Dino Molinaro back into the lineup. For “A Dark Beauty”, released 17 July 2026 through Dark Vinyl Records, the band worked as a trio of Aliani on vocals and electronics, Molinaro on bass and Ivan Bullock on guitar and electronics, with Ernie Oppenheimer producing, mixing and mastering. Guest contributions come from Vaselyne‘s Yvette Winkler and Paradox Obscur‘s Kriistal Ann on the album’s remix section, extending the darker, guitar-forward direction the band set on its previous release.

items.body: Being yourself has become a surprisingly laborious business. The photograph needs editing, the opinion needs prompting, and loneliness must be presented to resemble an enviable evening. A social media profile offers the freedom to create the person we wish we were, then puts that person to work around the clock. Before long, algorithmic approval starts behaving like a drug, desire becomes a recurring payment, and the supposedly liberated individual is checking in with the platform every few minutes. The mask has developed an excellent social life, but its owner could probably use some company. Berlin’s XTR HUMAN, the long-running project of musician Johannes Stabel, turns that predicament into a forceful EBM workout on “Fake,” shared ahead of its October 9 release through Wie Ein Gott Records. The first release in a new series, the single was recorded at Infinite Power Studios in Los Angeles, with Matia Simovich handling production and mixing. Its entirely analog construction puts the emphasis on force, repetition, and the persuasive pull of an electronic beat. “Fake” opens with a metallic bass synth line that gives its EBM groove a distinctly funky gait. There is plenty of force in the repetition, though the low end knows how to move its hips. Stabel’s vocals land with a slap, a club-driven Neue Deutsche Welle drawl carrying the rhythmic confidence and insolent phrasing of hip-hop. He makes each phrase feel physically involved in the beat, pushing the groove forward with a delivery that sounds thoroughly pleased with its own bad intentions. The synth melody brings to mind the peculiar electronic funk of Fad Gadget’s “Lady Shave,” while the track’s muscular structure shares more with the disciplined body music of fellow Mute artists DAF and Nitzer Ebb. Simovich’s production keeps those elements sharply defined: the bass has weight, the rhythm has room to work, and the melody provides enough mischief to make the machinery feel dangerously inviting. That invitation is central to the song’s themes. “Fake” confronts digital isolation, manufactured identities, and the ease with which desire becomes dependency. Profiles turn into disguises; the pursuit of recognition keeps the person behind them performing. The track’s repeated patterns give that cycle a bodily form, suggesting the exhausting business of moving constantly while getting nowhere. Stabel makes the predicament sound seductive, which is precisely how such arrangements secure our cooperation in the first place. Listen to “Fake” below: “Fake” is out October 9, 2026 via Wie Ein Gott Records. Find the single here on release day. Alongside Simovich’s production and mixing, the recording credits include assistant engineers Coleman Ketchem and Grover Greenberg, with mastering by Bonati Mastering. Johannes Stabel began XTR HUMAN in 2012, developing a project whose early coldwave and post-punk interests have expanded into industrial electronics, techno, and EBM. His rich vocal delivery gives those harder rhythms a recognizable personality, drawing together German-language phrasing, new wave melody, and the propulsion of body music. Albums such as G.O.L.D in 2021 and Schrank in 2024 established a catalogue equally interested in dancefloor movement and social criticism. Earlier this year, the Rave God EP brought ’90s rave energy into that combination, including a remix by Houses of Heaven. Stabel’s international live history includes Wave-Gotik-Treffen and Absolution Festival, alongside appearances with artists including Die Selektion, Qual, Lebanon Hanover, and She Past Away. This month’s shows include a return to Los Angeles for Substance at The Belasco, followed by Berlin’s Unterwelt Festival on Halloween. Upcoming 2026 live dates: October 8 — Denton, TX — Rubber Gloves Rehearsal Studios October 9 — Austin, TX — Cheer Up Charlies (NITE SCHOOL) October 15 — Spokane, WA — Red Room Lounge October 16 — Portland, OR — The Coffin (Halloween Fetish Ball) October 17 — Seattle, WA — The Mountain Room October 24 — Los Angeles, CA — The Belasco (Substance) October 31 — Berlin, Germany — Festsaal Kreuzberg (Unterwelt Festival) Follow XTR HUMAN: Website Facebook Instagram YouTube Bandcamp Spotify Cover photograph by Anni Porrasmäki. items.body: “Some endings don’t wait They arrive before you do” There is a peculiar humiliation in realizing that a relationship has ended while you were still making plans for it. Familiar routines can keep the illusion going for weeks: another message, another evening together, another promise you have learned to accept without examining too closely. Then some ordinary detail makes the situation impossible to explain away, and you find yourself catching up with a loss that has already happened. It’s the emotional equivalent of arriving late to a funeral party: the bar is empty, and the deviled eggs are already gone, and yet you’re still expecting the deceased to call you back. That liminal stretch between an ending and the moment you finally recognize it is the pulse of “No Flowers in June,” the latest single from Italian darkwave duo Soft Scent. A frantic bassline drives relentlessly onward as the synths press in around it, giving the track the jittery resolve of someone who’s just realized that standing still may be the worst thing to do. Moving on takes effort—especially when some part of you is still waiting for the other person to show up. Anna “MissLucifer” and Sara “Felina Noir” formed Soft Scent in 2023 in Italy’s Marche region, and the track is the first single from their forthcoming second album, Mother’s Ruin. Its restless movement draws on coldwave, old EBM, post-punk, the clipped propulsion of punk, and a glossy electronic abrasion that keeps the familiar ingredients feeling unsettled. At odd moments, the song seems to sit somewhere between Björk and Sigue Sigue Sputnik, which sounds ridiculous until you hear the vocal drama and synthetic sleaze brushing past one another. The song is about an ending, although not one of those glamorous endings rock music usually prefers. Nobody is smashing a mirror or walking dramatically into traffic. This is the more common variety: the thing is already over, and you are late to your own realization. Soft Scent refuses to overplay the tragedy. The arrangement holds its dark-disco poise: the bass stays restless, the electronics keep the pressure on. The hurt is unmistakable, but the song never crumples theatrically to make its point. That restraint cuts deeper than a dozen grand breakdowns ever could. The song’s video sets the band on a shadow-drenched stage, purple light pooling around them as candles and flowers frame the scene. It might have slipped into goth by numbers, but something stranger stirs—especially beside the album’s dried and ceramic blooms, and its Victorian Lover’s Eye imagery. Romance has survived, it seems, though never unwatched. Watch the video for No Flowers in June below: The title of Soft Scent’s forthcoming second studio album, Mother’s Ruin, comes from the old Victorian name for gin, which gives the album its larger framework: comfort and damage sharing the same glass. “No Flowers in June” fits neatly into that idea because it concerns the moment after escape has stopped working. You get your temporary relief, your little private holiday from consequence, and eventually consequence finds the forwarding address. No Flowers In June was recorded with Gianluca Lo Presti and mixed and mastered by William Faith, and thankfully nobody has polished it into sterility. It still has elbows. It still has that slightly unfriendly quality good dark music ought to possess. Soft Scent are not reinventing darkwave here, and that is probably beside the point. They are doing something more difficult. They are making it sound like it still has somewhere to go. Mother’s Ruin is expected in late 2026. In the meantime, order No Flowers in June here. items.body: Syndey Valette I Fucking Love You Artoffact Records I Fucking Love You represents a pretty big swing for Paris’ Sydney Valette. Where his material has always leaned into the history of dignified continental darkwave, Valette has never been afraid to inject some urgency, emotion and a dollop of dry humor into the proceedings. For this record he’s kicked those instincts into overdrive, making the most lively and varied album of his career to date. It’s a tightrope to maintain his measured approach to composition and performance while also letting those qualities that have previously been around the edges take a more direct spotlight, and Valette walks it with confidence and skill. Part of the record’s personality comes from how lively and ready to go the songs sound; not minimal by any means, but not overly ornamented or overworked. Opener “Warrior” is made up of a chirpy synth lead that has an almost futurepop sound, paired with a simple kick-clap drum pattern to drive it, his grave vocals, vocoder and samples from The Exorcist to fill it out. It’s effective because it’s simple and dramatic without seeming crass, a quality shared by such cuts as “Relèves-toi” whose mute pulsing bassline is punctuated by bursts of timpani and synthesized pipes, grand and even cinematic in scope, but not crowded or excessive. And when Valette really goes for the vocal gusto on the title track’s widescreen synthpop, dropping his often grave vocal delivery for a wounded croon and yelped and shouted backing, he keeps the speedy synths and drums behind him, giving himself the push and momentum for take-off. Whether those canny arrangement and delivery choices are instinctual or the product of hours of work, they really do make I Fucking Love You the album it is. Russian language cut “Как Свеча” certainly has the gravity inherent to the language as sung, and chooses to lay back in delivering its chorus, creating a tension between its melancholic and funereal mood and its zippy tempo. In perhaps the album’s most ambitious moment, closer “No Ibiza For Mr. Valette”, he goes with a plainer vocal style and uses some of his dry humor to play off what is clearly a song of heartbreak, the song slowly graduating from simple synths and drums to lush pads. Like the rest of the album, what makes it great is how it communicates so much emotionally and thematically without needing to state anything openly, saying very little but telling us everything. Buy it. I Fucking Love You by Sydney Valette The post Sydney Valette, “I Fucking Love You” appeared first on I Die: You Die.

items.body: Claudio Dondo began making music in the late 1980s. This path eventually led him to Runes Order, the project under which he has released countless recordings on a wide variety of labels since 1992. He has now joined forces with the German label Dark Vinyl Records and, much like on his previous album, initiated a collaboration with Regen Graves. We are presented with a total of 13 tracks. While the influences are highly eclectic, they can largely be categorized within genres such as Cinematic and Krautrock. The inclusion of additional guest musicians adds further diversity—for instance, on one track, a saxophone creates a wonderfully dark, Jazzy atmosphere. I wasn’t surprised to find references to John Carpenter’s films, yet this album offers far more than just Cinematic soundscapes. From vintage drum machine tones to driving rhythms, and from organ passages to analog effects, this work has a great deal to offer. Add to this a variety of vocal tracks alongside the instrumentals, and the result is a fascinating work that keeps the listener firmly in its grip. This is a varied and accomplished opus containing a few real gems. (Rating:7½). Listen to “Bury The Fetus”: Bury The Fetus by Runes Order & Regen Graves About Runes Order & Regen Graves Runes Order & Regen Graves is the collaboration between Claudio Dondo’s long-running Italian dark ambient project Runes Order, based in the Genoa area, and Regen Graves, a musician from the same Genoa scene known as a member of the horror-doom band Abysmal Grief. Dondo started the project in 1988 as Order 1968 and renamed it Runes Order in 1992 with the cassette “The Dream Door”. His catalogue includes “La Seduzione Del Silenzio” (1994), “Room 39” (1995), “The Art of Scare and Sorrow” (2002) and “Fase XIV” (2019), drawing on the cosmic and Berlin School tradition of Tangerine Dream, Faust and Klaus Schulze. Dondo and Regen Graves first joined forces on “Falsche Fragen” in 2023. “Escape”, their second album together, followed in 2026 on Dark Vinyl Records, pairing Berlin School electronics with horror and thriller soundtrack atmospheres across the thirteen tracks reviewed here.
items._genre: dark ambient / cinematic / krautrock / Berlin School
items._cn_summary: 这张专辑是意大利暗潮音乐人Claudio Dondo（以Runes Order之名活跃多年）与Regen Graves的第二次合作，由德国小众厂牌Dark Vinyl Records发行。整张作品共收录13首曲目，融合了电影配乐般的氛围铺陈与Krautrock的律动结构，合成器序列与模拟音效交织，辅以风琴段落和老式鼓机音色。部分曲目加入萨克斯独奏，呈现出阴暗的爵士质感；另有人声作品与纯器乐曲穿插。乐评将其与John Carpenter的电影配乐风格相提并论，同时强调其在电影化音景之外还提供了更多层次的内容。整体编排丰富且具吸引力，被描述为一部变化多样且完成度高的作品，其中包含若干出色的亮点段落。

items._cn_summary: 7FO新专辑延续其独特创作脉络，灵感源于日常生活中拾得石块突然碎裂的记忆片段。作品以纽埃吉式浮游感作为入口，营造出陌生却又莫名亲切的声景空间。音乐在飘渺的质地中展开，既不追求旋律的清晰可循，也不依赖传统结构，而是让声音本身成为叙事载体——奇异、不羁，却带着一种贴近体温的温度感。整体氛围介于迷幻与日常之间，弦外之音与具象声响交错，构成一幅难以归类的听觉图景。作为EM厂牌发行的新作，延续了2016年旧作再版后的海外关注势头，继续拓展其难以复制的个人化声学世界。

items.body: Can we really imagine death from a love? It’s one of those rare things that happens all too often, painted into the fabric of cotton goods promises and soft-hearted tenderness. Say a love leaves us unexpectedly, dies suddenly, and we are insatiable to that love originally – that could be marked as death from a love. Like something inside us has died, ready to be replaced with something else that we don’t really want to replace at all costs. This is the “love” element, closeness, some would say clinging, but I don’t know about you, love never comes through death… And I don’t know either, whether you also feel how mental transmogrification turns the concept of “it” inside out, with fake society, conceited people, counterfeit claims and all that negative mind-melting stuff that comes through death. Do some people enjoy perverting the concept of death? Of over-dramatising what life is actually always eternal? Seriousness is seriousness, and words are just that – dust in deserts of sound. It is only when we find material serious and mature enough to tranquilise the sheer grief that non-psycopathic people feel that we find albums like “Death From A Love”. It’s a great title, a great album and a great package. One that will last for all eternity in the eyes of those willing to use that oh-so important word: care. You need patience, in other words, to tackle a concept like “Death From A Love”. The weak-minded fall down and have no patience. The creator of this recording has a lot of patience, I would wager. How else could one commit to things that are seen as trite in the minds of the unminded robot-hybrids of our generation? Pedalling out the unreal at every turn – this album is real. From the opening lines, where morose tones touch the back of the neck in a FareWell Poetry style, the anger that we all feel is self-contained and instead of being left to fester, is expressed in musical, and here, reviewer language. It’s the least trade-off a true artist could expect of intelligent life, after all. As represented by electronic skeletons throughout the central coda. In life, nobody is better than anyone else. We are all winners. And every album is a treasure, whether you choose to “like” it or not? And what is like? We may as well be all self-defeatist – I’ll tell you what; we may as well all be Franz Kafka. Never finishing our stories properly – I’ve wrote a lot of those stories over the years. But the deciding factor on whether we keep art in our collections (we are ultimately nerdy collectors if we are perusing this area of music by nature, after all) is if the central concept is a successfully realised one. Come tune in to “Death From A Love” and find out why we have something special. www.homeassemblymusic.bandcamp.com

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑围绕'爱之死'概念展开，以阴郁的电子音景和极简化的音乐语言探讨失去与精神蜕变。评论指出开篇以低沉抑郁的音色触及听者颈背，类似FareWell Poetry式的氛围营造，而中段则出现电子骨架般的声音结构。整张作品拒绝戏剧化地渲染死亡，转而以克制、成熟的方式处理哀恸情绪。创作者展现出足够的耐心与投入，使得那些常被视为陈腐的主题获得新的重量。专辑在Bandcamp平台发行，属于独立小厂牌发行渠道，适合愿意花时间消化概念的听者。文中强调成功实现核心概念是评判艺术收藏价值的关键，这张作品在概念执行层面获得了肯定。

items.body:
After the OĽUN album I reviewed enthusiastically a while back, here’s the next project, again motivated and led by violinist/fiddler/composer Ján Kružliak Jr., continuing the rapprochement, indeed embrace, between Slovakia’s traditional music and its classical music. This time it reconnects the works of classical composers who were inspired by and drew on village musics with those traditional sources and styles.
Three ensembles are involved: the Spectrum Quartett led by Kru�liak with two violins, viola and cello; Nogaband, the traditional-style quartet of fiddles, contra (chording viola) and bass that’s led by fiddler and singer Michal Noga; and the female vocal group Ulijanky, plus guest singer Simona Hulejov�.
The majority of the tracks are interpretations of works by Slovak composer Eugen Suchon (1908-1993), with others from fellow-Slovaks Ilja Zeljenka (1932-2007) and Alexander Moyzes (1906-1984), and Hungarian B�la Bart�k (1881-1945) who did a lot of his very detailed collecting of folk music in Slovakia.
In each case the sources - musicians and locations in villages across Slovakia - are credited in the notes, and these arrangements and performances reconnect with the energy and traditional vocal sound of those sources.
In no way is this an orchestra-smoothed thing; this is gutsy, brilliantly played and sung music with all the spirit, skill and technique of traditional music, from players and singers who deeply understand and inhabit it. It’s a glorious piece of work, music to luxuriate in. There’s too much richness to begin to detail, but here’s a dip into a few moments to give the flavor. The tracks all have very long titles detailing their sources, so for brevity’s sake I’ll just give track numbers.

items._cn_summary: 这张专辑由小提琴家兼作曲家Ján Kružliak Jr.主导，延续其将斯洛伐克传统民间音乐与古典音乐相融合的路线。专辑汇聚三组乐团——以Kružliak为核心的Spectrum弦乐四重奏、由小提琴手Michal Noga带领的民间风格的Nogaband四重奏，以及女声合唱团Ulijanky，另有嘉宾歌手参与。曲目主要改编自斯洛伐克作曲家Eugen Suchoň、Ilja Zeljenka、Alexander Moyzes，以及曾在斯洛伐克大量采集民间音乐的匈牙利作曲家巴托克的作品。每首作品都标注了所借鉴的村落音乐来源与演奏者，使改编根植于真实的传统语境。整体演奏充满民间音乐的粗犷能量与真挚情感，而非古典乐团式的精致打磨，将民间旋律与人声传统重新注入室内乐框架，展现出深厚的文化根基与演奏功底。

items.body:
Though this recording documents the work of thirteen of Belgium's most innovative ensembles, the real star is the Park Abbey located just outside Leuven and founded in 1129. Built and maintained for the purpose of quiet meditation, the abbey hosted the musicians who used the quiet surroundings to prepare and record their unique musical imaginings. The result is a mostly instrumental collection that mines the riches of Belgian folk and world music traditions, including Romani scales,
La Pump
rhythms, and accordion-based
bal-musette
flavors.
For example, Slovenian-native R�n�lius Bikar�s searing violin opens the set with �R�fuge.� He and his self-named ensemble channel pan-European Roma history.
Meanwhile, �Poor Boy� is a Django Reinhardt-inspired swing tune by Charlotte Pelgen & Bipolar Bows. Pelgen sings in English, and with her ukulele strumming sounding very much like a tenor banjo, the tune is enlivened by Lotte Remmen�s St�phane Grappelli-like fiddle lines.
The distinctive sound of the oud announces yet another musical tradition. Blending Mediterranean with Arabic sounds, the Lebanese-Belgian singer Amber Haddad and her trio, oudist Adil Benhsain and double bassist Martijn Vanbuel, spin a beguiling musical web. According to the liner notes (translated from the Dutch), �Tawazden� is about �seeking balance and finding peace within a complex environment.� Further, �the various spaces of the abbey and their murals are the direct source of inspiration.�
The accordion is especially prominent. So too is the Western classical tradition. Sounding almost Baroque, �Sacristia Invisibilis,� is another standout for me. Here, mandolinist Andries Boone is joined by Anouk Sanczuk on octave violin (sometimes called the baritone violin, tuned an octave lower than standard) and on harpsichord Sandra Van der Gucht. They create an indescribable sound you have to hear.
Throughout, the Abbey�s stone presence looms. Aur�lie Charneux�s solo clarinet piece �L'Ape Millenaria� is about a thousand-year-old bee that haunts the abbey. �Thila,� by Enara Navaira, evokes ancient Celts with a jazzy double bass and drum kit behind throat singing and Citera (a kind of Hungarian zither).
Airboxes is a duo who mix chromatic and diatonic accordions. Their offering �Abdij 1� sounds improvised. Again from the liner notes, �they share their impressions of the timelessness of monastic life.�
Despite the wide range of styles,
The Sound of the Abbey
has a coherence, perhaps informed by the artists� shared inspiration. The record is often surprising and always soothing. Three years in the making, the ensembles were lovingly recorded and mixed by Bert Huysentruyt and mastered by Pieter De Wagter from Equus Mastering. They have rendered a warm sound using the natural reverb of ancient stone provided by the project�s silent partner.

(Interview)

Songbooks Live
(Review)

items._cn_summary: 这张合辑收录了比利时十三支创新乐团的作品，录制于1129年建立的鲁汶郊外帕克修道院。乐手们利用修道院的宁静环境和天然石质混响进行创作，呈现出以器乐为主的丰富面貌。曲目跨越罗姆人小提琴传统、Django Reinhardt风格的吉普赛摇摆、黎巴嫩-比利时融合的地中海与阿拉伯之声、手风琴与巴洛克元素的室内乐重奏，以及匈牙利扬琴与喉音演唱的古老凯尔特意象。评论特别提到几首突出曲目：小提琴家Rénélis Bikar以炽烈弓弦开启专辑；Charlotte Pelgen以尤克里里模仿四弦班卓琴营造复古摇摆；Amber Haddad与乌德琴、贝斯三重奏探讨平衡与平和；Andries Boone的曼陀林与拨弦古钢琴组合创造难以描述的听觉空间。这张耗时三年的作品在多元风格中保持了内在统一性，整体氛围既出人意料又令人舒缓，录音品质温暖自然。

items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. Further reading: Petrona Mart�nez - Ancestras (Review) Gnonnas Pedro & His Dadjes - Roi De L'Agbadja Moderne 1974-1983 (Review)

items._cn_summary: Analog Africa厂牌将贝宁传奇乐团Orchestre Poly-Rythmo的1977至1982年录音集结呈现，重点聚焦与作曲家Antoine Dougbé的合作。Dougbé以击打大腿的Cavacha节奏著称，该节奏由鼓手Belobi Meridjo从火车韵律中提炼，后席卷1970年代中期的刚果流行乐坛。Dougbé被称作'魔鬼首相'，作为伏都教信徒，他只与Poly-Rythmo合作，认为其他乐队无法精准呈现其构想。专辑录音年代跨越70年代末至80年代初，音色呈现时代特征——吉他带有塑料光泽，合成器开始进入编曲，但音乐根基仍扎在70年代。曲风中古巴son的影响较此前Poly-Rythmo合辑更为明显，刚果伦巴的痕迹亦清晰可闻。《Ma Won Min Towe Leo》以合成器铺底，闪光吉他与镲片主导节奏交织推进；《We Tayi Sin Assi Tche》则更直白地展现古巴色彩，铃鼓、尖锐人声对唱与紧密重复的吉他riff构成典型结构。这张合辑填补了Dougbé短暂但高浓度的创作生涯的记录空白。

items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Find the artist online. Further reading: Tako Toki - Hirsute Farfelus (Review) Terje Isungset - Glacial Poetry (Review)

items._cn_summary: Tako Toki的第二张专辑延续了首张作品的多元文化融合路线，核心特色在于全部使用自制的非常规乐器演奏——包括tassofons、kitchenofon等由废旧物品改造的装置，却展现出惊人的音准精度与丰富音色。乐评依次介绍了各曲风格来源：开篇曲目借鉴克莱兹默传统，簧乐器与小幽默的人声呼应；中段作品融入库姆比亚节奏与西班牙合唱；同名曲以非洲节拍的木鱼、沙锤构建律动，旋律线由马林巴琴引出；终段回归桑巴与中东迷幻旋律。整张专辑以嬉戏态度呈现跨文化音乐实验，既致敬世界各地对节奏与旋律的热爱，也提醒音乐人不拘于器物本身。

items.body: After the extra-terrestial explorations of Eventyrferd , the previous album from Norway's Camilla Hole Trio, in which sci-fi synth sounds were married with traditional material, their latest release Langs is rather more earthbound. But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio

items._cn_summary: 挪威Camilla Hole Trio在专辑《Langs》中将传统挪威民间素材与爵士即兴手法相结合。主奏乐器高音萨克斯在保留民间旋律骨架的同时，融入了自由即兴段落，贝斯手与鼓手不断切换角色，打破传统主奏-伴奏的固定配置。模块化合成器与颤音琴的叠加为传统民间舞曲注入了现代声响色彩，使作品在保持地域文化根基的同时展现出开放的音乐视野。乐队在继承挪威西海岸民间传统的基础上，对乐器编制和即兴结构进行持续探索，形成了一种兼具民俗根基与实验精神的融合风格。

I want to personally direct you to a remarkable piece of music titled "Two Views of a Prayer," composed and written by
David Dzubinski
as part of the
Prism Quartet
's new series of collaborations called
Unlocking Your Inner Composer
. If you have listened to my radio programs, you are probably familiar with the quartet's ground-breaking, genre-blurring music. If not, there's no better introduction than this.
Performed in November of 2025 at the Free Library of Philadelphia, they invited vocalist
Ursula Rucker
, percussionist
Tyshawn Sorey
, and violinist
Carlos Santiago
